title: Design a Live Commenting System
prompt:
Design the live comment stream under a broadcast video. Viewers post short comments and everyone watching sees new comments appear within a second or two. Late joiners see recent comments, and the comments remain attached to the video for replay afterwards.

Assume a single popular stream can have **1 million concurrent viewers** and **5,000 new comments per second** at its peak, with many thousands of streams live at once.
clarify: Must every viewer see every comment, or is a representative sample acceptable on huge streams?
Do comments need to be strictly ordered, or is approximate order fine?
Is moderation required before display (spam filter, blocked words, banned users)?
Do replies, reactions and pinned comments count, or only flat text?
What happens after the stream: are comments replayed in sync with the video?

reference.requirements:
**Functional**
- Post a short comment to a live stream (auth required)
- Everyone watching sees new comments in near real time
- Late joiners get the latest N comments
- Comments are stored and replayable by video time

**Non-functional**
- Delivery latency 1–2 s end to end
- A viral stream must not hurt other streams (isolation)
- Writes are bursty and spam-prone; protect the system
- Availability over strict consistency: dropping some comments on overload is acceptable
reference.estimation:
- Hot stream: 1M viewers, 5,000 comments/s
- Naive fanout: 5,000 × 1M = **5 billion deliveries/s**, which is impossible and also unreadable by a human
- Humans read ~20 comments/s at most, so cap what each viewer receives at 20/s: 1M × 20 = 20M comment-deliveries/s, batched as one frame per viewer per second
- Bandwidth: 20 comments × 100 B = 2 KB/viewer/s × 1M = **2 GB/s ≈ 16 Gbps** for this one stream
- Gateways: 1M connections at ~100k per host ≈ **10 gateways** for the stream; storage: 5,000/s × 150 B ≈ 0.75 MB/s ≈ 65 GB/day for a stream this hot
reference.api:
```
POST /v1/streams/{id}/comments   {client_id, text}    → 202 {comment_id}
GET  /v1/streams/{id}/comments?around=<video_ts>&limit=50   (late joiners, replay)
SSE/WS /v1/streams/{id}/live      ← batched frames: {comments[], server_ts}
```
- `202` because the comment is accepted for moderation and fanout, not yet delivered.
- Server-Sent Events fit well: traffic is one-way server to client, it works over plain HTTP/2 and reconnects with `Last-Event-ID`.
reference.data:
- `comments(stream_id, comment_id, user_id, text, video_offset_ms)` in a wide-column or partitioned store, keyed by `stream_id` and ordered by `comment_id` (time-sortable). A very hot stream is further bucketed by time window to avoid one giant partition.
- Recent window: per stream a capped list of the latest ~200 comments in Redis for late joiners.
- Moderation state: per-user mute/ban set and a blocked-terms list.
- Stream → gateway subscriptions are held in the pub/sub layer, not in the database.
reference.design:
```
viewer ─POST▶ API ─▶ rate limit ─▶ moderation ─▶ comment queue (partition by stream_id)
                                                    │
                          ┌─────────────────────────┤
                          ▼                         ▼
                    store (history)         stream aggregator (sample/batch ≤20/s)
                                                    │ publish
                                       pub/sub topic per stream
                                    ┌────────┴────────┐
                                gateway 1 … gateway N ─▶ 100k viewers each
```
- A **fanout tree**: one aggregator per stream feeds N gateways, each fanning out to its local viewers. Posting never touches viewer connections directly.
reference.deepdives:
- **Fan-out at one million viewers.** The cost is viewers × rate, so cut the rate. The aggregator batches per 500 ms to 1 s window and, above ~20 comments/s, samples (prefer comments from followed accounts, verified users and high-quality ones). Every viewer gets the same frame, so it is built once, published once per gateway, and written to each socket. Trade-off: not every comment is seen live; all remain in storage.
- **Push transport and scale.** SSE/WebSocket keeps a connection per viewer; the alternative is polling a CDN-cached "latest comments" object every 2 s, which scales to huge audiences via cache but adds latency and request volume. Use a hybrid: polling for cold or massive streams, push for the rest. Reconnect with jitter and resume from the last comment id.
- **Ordering and hot partitions.** Time-sortable ids give approximate order; strict order across servers is unnecessary since only the aggregator decides frame order. A hot stream gets its own queue partition(s) and aggregator, so it cannot starve small streams.
- **Abuse.** Per-user rate limits (e.g. 1 comment per second), spam classifiers inline, shadow-banning so spammers do not learn they were blocked.
reference.wrapup:
- The central idea is to bound per-viewer delivery with batching and sampling, then fan out through a tree of aggregators and gateways.
- Trade-offs: completeness vs readability and cost, push vs CDN polling, inline vs async moderation.
- Next: reactions, pinned comments, multi-region gateways, replay sync with video time.

rubric.text: Does the fanout arithmetic (comments/s × viewers) and concludes naive delivery is infeasible
Caps and batches per-viewer delivery: sampling or rate-limiting what each client receives
Decouples posting from delivery with a queue partitioned by stream
Uses a fanout tree: aggregator per stream, then gateways each serving a share of connections
Chooses a transport and justifies it: SSE or WebSocket push, possibly with CDN-cached polling for huge streams
Provides late-joiner catch-up from a capped recent-comments cache
Stores comments durably, keyed by stream and a time-sortable id, with video offset for replay
Handles hot streams: isolation, dedicated partitions/aggregators, time-bucketed partitions
Covers abuse protection: rate limiting, spam/moderation inline, shadow ban
Accepts best-effort delivery under overload (shed load rather than fail), and handles reconnect with resume ids
